sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    N1[1] --> N2[2] --> N3[3] --> NIL[nil]
    R[reverse] --> P1[prev=nil, curr=1]
    P1 --> S1[next=2, 1.Next=nil]
    S1 --> P2[prev=1, curr=2]
    P2 --> S2[next=3, 2.Next=1]
    S2 --> P3[prev=2, curr=3]
    P3 --> S3[next=nil, 3.Next=2]
    S3 --> D[done: 3→2→1→nil]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The pointer mechanics, one layer down: curr.Next = prev is one store — reversing a node is a single pointer write. The total cost is O(n) — one loop, no allocation. Space: O(1) — the three variables, regardless of list length. That's the property that makes in-place reversal the canonical interview question: trivial invariant, trivial loop, and every line must be right.

The recursive alternative and its trade: recurse to the tail, then flip on the way back (head.Next.Next = head; head.Next = nil). Same O(n) time, but O(n) stack space — the loop version is strictly better for the general case. The recursive version maps cleanly to the problem's structure (the reversed tail is the subproblem), which is why interviews ask for both.

The Go-specific pattern: the singly-linked list with methods (func (n *Node) Len() int, func (n *Node) String() string) — the type reads as a package-level utility. The container/list package (doubly-linked) exists for when you genuinely need O(1) insertion/removal — rare in application code.
